why: Producers trap solar energy via photosynthesis, forming the base of every food chain.

q: Organisms that eat herbivores directly are called:
why: Secondary consumers (carnivores) feed on primary consumers (herbivores).

q: According to the 10% law of energy flow, if producers have 1000 units of energy, how much reaches the primary consumers?
why: Only about 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level: 10% of 1000 = 100.

q: A food web, compared to a single food chain, gives an ecosystem:
o: Greater stability due to alternate feeding links
why: Interconnected food chains in a web allow organisms alternate food sources if one link is lost.

q: An ecological pyramid of numbers, biomass, or energy represents data at successive:
why: Ecological pyramids depict numbers/biomass/energy across trophic levels from producers upward.

q: The gradual, directional change in species composition of a community over time is called:
why: Succession is the stepwise replacement of communities until a stable climax community forms.

q: In the carbon cycle, CO2 is returned to the atmosphere mainly through:
why: Respiration by organisms and combustion of fuels release CO2 back into the atmosphere.

q: Atmospheric nitrogen is converted into a usable form for plants mainly by:
why: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium) convert N2 gas into ammonia/nitrates usable by plants.

q: A food chain that begins with dead organic matter rather than living plants is called a:
why: Detritus food chains start from dead organic matter broken down by decomposers.

q: Decomposers play their key ecological role by:
o: Breaking down dead matter and releasing nutrients back to soil
why: Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients from dead organisms back into the ecosystem.
